subject: Respiratory
vignette: A 22-year-old man presents with sudden onset of right-sided chest pain and dyspnea after exercising. He is tachypneic. The right chest expands less than the left; percussion is hyperresonant on the right, tactile fremitus is decreased, and breath sounds are diminished on the right.
question: Which of the following best explains these physical examination findings?

options.text: Air in the right pleural space, which is hyperresonant to percussion and reduces transmission of fremitus and breath sounds.
Fluid in the right pleural space, which is dull to percussion and increases tactile fremitus.
Consolidation of the right lung, which produces dullness and increased fremitus.
Pleural thickening from prior inflammation, which is dull to percussion but hyperresonant on inspiration.
Bilateral hyperinflation from asthma, with symmetric wheezing and equal chest expansion.

explanation_correct: Pneumothorax is air in the pleural space. The affected side is hyperresonant to percussion because air replaces normal lung tissue density, and tactile fremitus and breath sounds are diminished because the collapsed lung and intervening air transmit sound poorly. Uneven chest expansion is also classic. These findings distinguish pneumothorax from pleural effusion (dullness) and consolidation (dullness with increased fremitus).

explanation_incorrect.B: A pleural effusion produces dullness to percussion, not hyperresonance, because fluid increases tissue density and changes sound transmission.
explanation_incorrect.C: Lobar consolidation produces dullness to percussion with increased tactile fremitus and bronchial breath sounds, the opposite of these findings.
explanation_incorrect.D: Pleural thickening or scarring is dull to percussion rather than hyperresonant and does not cause acute unilateral hyperresonance.
explanation_incorrect.E: Asthma causes bilateral, symmetric hyperresonance with diffuse wheezing, not unilateral findings with diminished breath sounds and uneven expansion.

educationalObjective: Pneumothorax produces unilateral hyperresonance, decreased tactile fremitus, diminished breath sounds, and uneven chest expansion on the affected side.

subject: Respiratory
vignette: A 19-year-old tall, thin male college student develops sudden left shoulder and chest pain while lifting weights. He is a tobacco smoker who also vapes. Chest x-ray shows a small left pneumothorax with a visible apical bleb; there is no history of lung disease or trauma.
question: Which of the following best characterizes this pneumothorax?

options.text: Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax due to bullae from emphysema.
Traumatic pneumothorax due to a rib fracture.
Tension pneumothorax with mediastinal shift away from the affected side.
Iatrogenic pneumothorax from central line placement.
Primary spontaneous pneumothorax from rupture of an apical subpleural bleb.

explanation_correct: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax occurs in patients without underlying lung disease, classically tall, thin young males, and is strongly associated with tobacco smoking and vaping. It results from rupture of apical subpleural blebs or cysts, allowing air to enter the pleural space. The absence of trauma, instrumentation, and chronic lung disease distinguishes it from other categories. Small cases may be observed, while larger ones are treated with aspiration or a chest tube.

explanation_incorrect.A: Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax occurs in patients with underlying lung disease (eg, emphysematous bullae, Marfan syndrome, infections); this patient has none.
explanation_incorrect.B: A traumatic pneumothorax requires injury such as a rib fracture or penetrating wound; none is described in this patient.
explanation_incorrect.C: Tension pneumothorax implies trapped air with mediastinal shift and obstructive physiology; a small apical bleb rupture without these findings is a simple primary spontaneous pneumothorax.
explanation_incorrect.D: Iatrogenic pneumothorax follows a medical procedure such as central venous catheter placement or lung biopsy; no procedure occurred here.

educationalObjective: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax affects tall, thin young males without underlying lung disease and results from rupture of an apical subpleural bleb, often related to smoking or vaping.

subject: Respiratory
vignette: A 70-year-old man with severe COPD and apical bullae develops sudden dyspnea and right-sided chest pain. Chest x-ray shows a right pneumothorax. There was no trauma and no medical procedure.
question: Which category of pneumothorax does this represent, and what predisposed to it?

options.text: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax from a ruptured apical bleb in a previously healthy person.
Traumatic pneumothorax from a rib fracture due to severe coughing.
Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax from rupture of a bulla in diseased lung.
Tension pneumothorax from a penetrating injury.
Iatrogenic pneumothorax from positive-pressure ventilation.

explanation_correct: Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax occurs in patients with underlying pulmonary disease. In emphysema, apical bullae can rupture and leak air into the pleural space. Other predisposing conditions include Marfan syndrome and pulmonary infections. The absence of trauma or instrumentation rules out traumatic and iatrogenic causes, and the presence of diseased lung distinguishes it from primary spontaneous pneumothorax. These patients often tolerate the pneumothorax poorly because of limited pulmonary reserve.

explanation_incorrect.A: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax requires the absence of underlying lung disease; this patient has severe COPD with bullae, so it is secondary spontaneous.
explanation_incorrect.B: Although severe coughing can precipitate an air leak, there is no evidence of a rib fracture or external trauma; the underlying mechanism is rupture of a diseased bulla.
explanation_incorrect.D: Tension pneumothorax is defined by trapped air and obstructive shock physiology, not by a penetrating injury; a penetrating injury would instead be a traumatic cause.
explanation_incorrect.E: An iatrogenic pneumothorax from positive-pressure ventilation requires mechanical ventilation with high pressures (barotrauma); this patient was not ventilated.

educationalObjective: Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax arises from rupture of diseased lung (eg, emphysematous bullae, Marfan syndrome, infection), often with more severe symptoms due to limited reserve.

subject: Respiratory
vignette: A 58-year-old man requires urgent central venous catheter placement in the right subclavian vein. Immediately after the procedure he develops sudden dyspnea. Chest x-ray shows air in the right pleural space with no rib fracture.
question: Which of the following best classifies this pneumothorax?

options.text: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax from a ruptured apical bleb.
Iatrogenic traumatic pneumothorax from central line placement.
Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax from an emphysematous bulla.
Tension pneumothorax from a gunshot wound.
Primary spontaneous pneumothorax related to vaping.

explanation_correct: Traumatic pneumothorax includes blunt injury (eg, rib fracture), penetrating injury (eg, gunshot), and iatrogenic causes. Iatrogenic pneumothorax is a well-known complication of central venous catheter placement, lung biopsy, and positive-pressure mechanical ventilation (barotrauma). The temporal relationship to subclavian central line placement and the absence of other causes make this an iatrogenic traumatic pneumothorax.

explanation_incorrect.A: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax occurs without any medical intervention or trauma; this pneumothorax followed a central line procedure.
explanation_incorrect.C: Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax arises from underlying lung disease such as emphysema; this event is procedure-related, not disease-related.
explanation_incorrect.D: A gunshot wound would be a penetrating traumatic cause; there was no penetrating injury here, only a central line.
explanation_incorrect.E: Vaping is associated with primary spontaneous pneumothorax in young people, but this patient's pneumothorax followed an invasive procedure.

educationalObjective: Iatrogenic pneumothorax is a form of traumatic pneumothorax caused by procedures such as central line placement, lung biopsy, or mechanical ventilation barotrauma.

subject: Respiratory
vignette: A 30-year-old man sustains a stab wound to the right chest. He becomes hypotensive (blood pressure 80/50 mm Hg) and tachycardic (heart rate 125/min), with jugular venous distention. Examination shows hyperresonance on the right, absent breath sounds, and tracheal deviation to the left.
question: Which hemodynamic mechanism best explains this patient's shock?

options.text: Blood loss causing hypovolemic shock from a large hemothorax.
Myocardial contusion causing cardiogenic shock.
Systemic vasodilation from severe pain causing distributive shock.
Increased intrathoracic pressure kinking the IVC, reducing venous return and cardiac output (obstructive shock).
Reduced arterial oxygen content from a simple pneumothorax alone causing shock.

explanation_correct: In tension pneumothorax, air enters the pleural space but cannot exit, so pressure accumulates. The markedly elevated intrathoracic pressure displaces the mediastinum away from the affected side and kinks the inferior vena cava, sharply reducing venous return. The fall in preload reduces cardiac output, producing obstructive shock with hypotension, tachycardia, and jugular venous distention. Tracheal deviation away from the affected lung is a classic sign, and immediate needle decompression is required.

explanation_incorrect.A: A hemothorax from a stab wound can cause hypovolemic shock, but hyperresonance rather than dullness, absent breath sounds, and tracheal deviation away from the affected side point to tension pneumothorax rather than blood in the pleural space.
explanation_incorrect.B: Myocardial contusion would cause cardiogenic shock with pulmonary edema and dullness to percussion; the examination here is that of a tension pneumothorax.
explanation_incorrect.C: Pain can produce vasovagal changes, but it does not create the obstructive physiology with jugular venous distention and tracheal deviation described here.
explanation_incorrect.E: A simple pneumothorax reduces oxygenation but does not obstruct venous return or cause obstructive shock; shock indicates progression to tension physiology.

educationalObjective: Tension pneumothorax causes obstructive shock because trapped pleural air raises intrathoracic pressure, kinks the IVC, reduces venous return, and lowers cardiac output.

subject: Respiratory
vignette: A 45-year-old woman is on mechanical ventilation for acute respiratory failure. Suddenly her peak airway pressures rise, her blood pressure falls, and her breath sounds become absent on the left with hyperresonance.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate next step?

options.text: Immediate needle decompression of the left pleural space, followed by chest tube placement.
Obtain a chest x-ray to confirm the diagnosis before any intervention.
Increase the FIO2 and administer an inhaled bronchodilator.
Perform a thoracentesis to remove the accumulated fluid.
Administer a loop diuretic to reduce presumed pulmonary edema.

explanation_correct: This ventilated patient has developed a tension pneumothorax from barotrauma: sudden deterioration, rising airway pressures, hypotension, absent breath sounds, and hyperresonance on the left. Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis requiring immediate needle decompression (needle thoracostomy), followed by definitive chest tube placement. Waiting for imaging would delay life-saving treatment.

explanation_incorrect.B: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical emergency; obtaining a chest x-ray before decompression can be fatal and is not recommended when the diagnosis is evident.
explanation_incorrect.C: Increasing FIO2 and giving a bronchodilator do not relieve the trapped pleural air or the obstruction to venous return.
explanation_incorrect.D: Thoracentesis removes fluid (eg, a pleural effusion); the problem here is air under pressure, requiring needle decompression and a chest tube.
explanation_incorrect.E: A loop diuretic treats pulmonary edema and transudative effusions by lowering hydrostatic pressure; it has no role in relieving a tension pneumothorax.

educationalObjective: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis requiring immediate needle decompression followed by chest tube placement; imaging must not delay treatment.

subject: Respiratory
vignette: A 25-year-old man presents after a motor vehicle accident with right-sided chest pain, dyspnea, tachycardia, and mild hypotension. Breath sounds are decreased on the right with hyperresonance, but the trachea is midline and there is no jugular venous distention.
question: Which feature, if it appeared, would most strongly indicate progression to a tension pneumothorax rather than a simple pneumothorax?

options.text: Decreased tactile fremitus on the affected side.
Hyperresonance to percussion on the affected side.
Uneven chest expansion between the two sides.
Diminished breath sounds over the affected side.
Tracheal deviation to the left (away from the affected right side) with worsening hypotension and jugular venous distention.

explanation_correct: Simple and tension pneumothorax share the local findings of hyperresonance, decreased fremitus, diminished breath sounds, and uneven expansion. Tension pneumothorax is distinguished by the systemic consequences of trapped, pressurized air: mediastinal shift with tracheal deviation away from the affected side, kinking of the IVC, reduced venous return, obstructive shock with hypotension and tachycardia, and jugular venous distention. Those features mandate immediate decompression.

explanation_incorrect.A: Decreased tactile fremitus occurs in any pneumothorax because pleural air impairs sound transmission; it does not distinguish simple from tension.
explanation_incorrect.B: Hyperresonance is a hallmark of all pneumothoraces and is not specific to tension physiology.
explanation_incorrect.C: Uneven chest expansion is a general feature of pneumothorax and does not indicate progression to tension.
explanation_incorrect.D: Diminished breath sounds over the affected side occur in both simple and tension pneumothorax and are not discriminating.

educationalObjective: Tracheal deviation away from the affected side, hypotension, and JVD distinguish tension from simple pneumothorax; local findings such as hyperresonance and diminished breath sounds are shared.
